noteBlocks.lede: Some differences between people come in a few separate kinds; others come in every size in between. One question, counted or measured, decides the name of the variation and the graph you draw. Then there is where the differences come from: genes, the environment, or both.

noteBlocks.md:
**Variation** is the differences between individuals in their **phenotype**, the characteristics each one actually has.

**Discontinuous variation** falls into a few **separate groups**, with nothing in between: **tongue rolling** and **hand dominance** are the examples.

**Continuous variation** can take **any value in a range**: **height** and **length** are the examples. You measure them, and every value in between is possible.

noteBlocks.prompt: Hand span is measured in centimetres and can be any value in a range. Which type of variation does it show?
noteBlocks.explain: Continuous: it is measured, and any value in between is possible. Discontinuous variation comes in separate groups, like tongue rolling.

noteBlocks.title: Why the classes read 160 to 165, then 165 to 170
noteBlocks.md: Each class runs from its lower value up to, but not including, its upper value. A height of exactly 165 cm goes in the 165 to 170 class, so every height has exactly one place and no gap is left.

noteBlocks.md:
**Worked example.** What percentage of this class is shorter than 160 cm?
**Step 1: read the bars.** The 150 to 155 bar holds 1 and the 155 to 160 bar holds 4. So 1 + 4 = 5 pupils are shorter than 160 cm.
**Step 2: find the whole class.** Add every bar: 28 pupils.
**Step 3: divide, then multiply by 100.** 5 ÷ 28 × 100 = 17.9%, to 1 decimal place.
Check: this is part of the class, so it must be under 100%.

noteBlocks.prompt: In a class of 25 pupils, 7 are left-handed. What percentage of the class is left-handed?
noteBlocks.explain: 7 ÷ 25 × 100 = 28%. The group goes on top and the whole class on the bottom.

noteBlocks.md:
Variation has a **genetic** basis and an **environmental** basis.

**Genetic.** A **mutation** is a **random change in the number of chromosomes or the structure of a gene**, so it can make something new. **Sexual reproduction** gives every child a new combination of its parents' genes. Both produce different phenotypes.

**Environmental.** Your surroundings shape how you develop: **diet** affects **height**, for example.

Most characteristics depend on both.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which two things give variation a genetic basis?
noteBlocks.explain: Mutation and sexual reproduction. Diet and exercise are part of the environment.

items.stem: Before we start, three things from earlier work. Nobody expects you to know this lesson yet. What is a gene?

options.text: a section of DNA that codes for one protein
options.feedback: A section of DNA that codes for one protein.
A chromosome carries many genes along its length.
That is part of your phenotype. The gene is the code behind it.

options.text: all the DNA in a cell
options.feedback: That is the genome.
Its characteristics: what it looks like and how it works. Variation is differences in phenotype.

options.text: the pair of alleles it carries
options.feedback: That is its genotype. The phenotype is what those alleles, and the environment, produce.
That is its genome.

options.text: the type of cell division that makes its gametes
options.feedback: That is meiosis.

items.stem: On which kind of graph do the bars touch?
items.skill: Recall the difference between a bar chart and a histogram (Mathematics)

options.feedback: A histogram. Its bars sit on a continuous number line, so they touch.
A bar chart's bars stand apart, one for each separate category.
A pie chart has no bars.
A line graph has points joined by a line, not bars.

items.stem: Which of these is an example of continuous variation?

options.feedback: Hand span is measured and can take any value in a range.
Blood group falls into four separate groups: discontinuous.
You can or you cannot: two separate groups, so discontinuous.
Left or right: separate groups, so discontinuous.

items.stem: Which graph should display the body masses of 30 pupils?
items.skill: Choose the graph for measured data

options.text: a histogram, with the bars touching
options.feedback: Body mass is continuous, so the bars touch: no mass falls between two classes.

options.text: a bar chart, with gaps between the bars
options.feedback: Gaps say there is nothing in between, but every mass in between is possible.
A pie chart shows shares of a whole, not how a measurement is spread.

options.text: a line graph joining each pupil's mass
options.feedback: The pupils are not in any order, so a line joining them means nothing. Group the masses into classes and draw a histogram.

items.stem: Which two things give variation a genetic basis?
items.skill: Name the genetic causes of variation

options.feedback: Mutation makes something new; sexual reproduction makes new combinations of what the parents have.
Those are environmental causes.
Mutation is genetic, but diet is environmental.
Sexual reproduction is genetic, but sunlight is part of the environment.

options.text: a random change in the number of chromosomes or the structure of a gene
options.feedback: A random change in the number of chromosomes or the structure of a gene.

options.text: a change caused by the environment, such as a scar
options.feedback: A scar is environmental and is not in the genes at all.

options.text: a change that always harms the organism
options.feedback: Most mutations have no noticeable effect; very few are harmful or useful.

options.text: a skill learned during an organism's life
options.feedback: A learned skill is not in the genes and is not passed on.

parts.stem: A class recorded their blood groups. State the type of variation shown by blood group, and give a reason for your answer.

accepted: discontinuous, because each person is in one of four separate groups with nothing in between

scheme.for: discontinuous

parts.workedSolution: Discontinuous, because each person is in one of four separate groups with nothing in between.

parts.stem: There are 30 pupils in the class. Use the bar chart to calculate the percentage of the class with blood group O. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
hints: Read the O bar, then divide by the whole class.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the percentage of the class who are not blood group O. Use the O bar on top of the fraction.
That divides the class by the group, so the fraction is upside down. A part of the class must come out below 100%.

parts.stem: The class also measured their hand spans. Name the type of graph that should be used to display the hand spans, and explain why.

accepted: a histogram, because hand span is continuous and can take any value in a range

scheme.for: histogram
hand span is continuous / can take any value in a range

hints: Hand span is measured with a ruler.
parts.workedSolution: A histogram, because hand span is continuous and can take any value in a range.

commonErrors.feedback: That graph suits data in separate groups, like the blood groups. Hand span can take any value, so it needs a histogram with the bars touching.

parts.stem: Hand span is affected by genes and by the environment. Suggest one environmental factor that could affect hand span.

accepted: the food a person eats as they grow

scheme.for: diet (accept: nutrition, injury, illness)

hints: Something outside the body that affects how it grows.
parts.workedSolution: Diet.

findTheMistake.stem: Ruth reads a bar chart showing 28 right-handed and 4 left-handed pupils. She is asked for the percentage of the class who are left-handed. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 is right. Line 2 turns the fraction upside down: it divides the class by the group. The group goes on top and the whole class on the bottom, which gives 12.5%.
findTheMistake.feedback: An answer of more than 100% for part of a class is the signal to look again. Summer 2025's B2 Foundation report records the same slip: candidates carried out a percentage calculation the wrong way round.

prompts.prompt: What is continuous variation, and which graph displays it?
prompts.answer: A characteristic that can take any value in a range, such as height. It is displayed on a histogram, with the bars touching.

prompts.prompt: What is discontinuous variation, and which graph displays it?
prompts.answer: A characteristic that falls into a few separate groups, such as tongue rolling. It is displayed on a bar chart, with gaps between the bars.

prompts.prompt: Why do the bars of a histogram touch but the bars of a bar chart do not?
prompts.answer: A histogram shows measured data: every value in between is possible, so one class runs into the next. A bar chart shows separate groups with nothing in between.

prompts.prompt: Name the two causes of variation that have a genetic basis.

prompts.answer: A random change in the number of chromosomes or in the structure of a gene.

prompts.prompt: Two cuttings from one plant grow to different heights. Why must the cause be environmental?
prompts.answer: Cuttings from one plant have the same genes, so any difference between them comes from the environment, such as water or light.
